top_choice_rationale: P001 (Helpman and Melitz, B010) has the most precisely identifiable core of the four proposals. That core is Melitz (2003) together with Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus foreign direct investment. The credit line has two names, so no cut falls inside the credited set. The framework has been tested on firm-level data from many countries for over twenty years. Cited as a theory of firm heterogeneity, selection and reallocation, it avoids claiming a welfare magnitude. It also avoids claiming discovery of the exporter-premia facts, which belong partly to the uncredited Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum lineage. I treat that gap as real but manageable through the citation wording. I rank P003 second because Autor, Dorn and Hanson are a coherent attribution unit with well-identified local labour-market evidence. Its costs are the debated magnitude and persistence of the effects and task-framework credit that lies outside the ballot. P004 comes third because its identification is partly observational and it overlaps in part with the 2024 prize. P002 comes fourth because eight credited names make any three-person cut contestable. The choice between honouring the theoretical originators and the estimation strand is also unresolved, and Phillips-curve evidence is mixed. I rank P000 last because every proposal describes a mature, substantive achievement. I have not counted supporter numbers as merit.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. None of Helpman, Melitz, Redding, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz, Persson, Tabellini, Besley, Calvo, Taylor or Woodford is a documented co-author. My field of empirical labour economics is closer to the B032 proposal than to B010, and I applied common criteria rather than treating proximity as merit. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
